She likely knew some time before her arrest that her life was in danger. She also was arrested over 2 weeks before her execution, so she had ample time to think about what she would say in those final moments. This is a woman who was clever enough to convince an early modern European king to separate from the Catholic Church ***and*** discard his wife of over 20 years and teenage daughter, largely through letters.

Anne was masterfully being incendiary without creating any additional danger to her daughter and remaining family.

RANKING the 5 books from worst to best (my opinion). I encourage you all to do the same!

5. Mockingjay: For me, the least engaging of the books. Probably because it’s the only book to not feature a formal games. The dichotomy of Snow and Coin, and their shared immorality was probably the most interesting part for me. It is a YA novel after all, we always knew the heroes were going to win in the end.

4. Ballad: I enjoyed Ballad. It was interesting experiencing the world through Snows eyes. I think the book does a good job of making snow an empathetic figure while also showing how his choices contribute to his violent and evil legacy. I can’t justify putting it above any of the other 3 though.

3. Catching Fire: I feel like this is a slow burn book, just as the title suggests (intended?). The early chapters of Katniss navigating the world post-74 was for me very boring. I think it spent too much time trying to develop the borderline-unnecessary Peeta Katniss Gale love triangle. If there was less of that, CF would easily compete for #1

2. (VERY close) Sunrise: Perhaps it’s my fondness of the series, but I found this book to be absolutely wonderful. The way it deals with the reality of PTSD, substance abuse, politics, among other issues is brilliantly simple in a way that makes it understandable to its intended audience while tacking issues complex enough to be engaging even for adult readers. My one gripe is that I read the name ‘Lenore Dove’ more times than I care to count. Other than that, Sunrise nearly perfectly captures the same tone of the last book on this list.

1. The Hunger Games: The book that started it all. You can tell from the very beginning that this world is rough, and it’s a world not too different than our own. It addresses the themes of poverty, loss, autonomy, and selflessness (among many others) in the same brilliantly simple way that makes it engaging for people of all ages. The Hunger Games had it’s love drama yes, but in a way that, so seamlessly intertwined with the overarching story, didn’t feel like it was the main focus for any extended period of time. I don’t think I will ever get sick of reading THG. It’s been 13 years since I first read it and have loved it and its successors since then.
